records.sourceHebrew: וְכָ֘כָה֮ תֹּאכְל֣וּ אֹתוֹ֒ מׇתְנֵיכֶ֣ם חֲגֻרִ֔ים נַֽעֲלֵיכֶם֙ בְּרַגְלֵיכֶ֔ם וּמַקֶּלְכֶ֖ם בְּיֶדְכֶ֑ם וַאֲכַלְתֶּ֤ם אֹתוֹ֙ בְּחִפָּז֔וֹן פֶּ֥סַח ה֖וּא לַיהֹוָֽה׃
records.sourceEnglish: This is how you shall eat it: your waist girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand. You shall eat it in haste; it is a Passover offering to the LORD.
records.targetHebrew: א] רֵאשִׁית כְּנִיסַת הָאָדָם לַעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת בְּחִפָּזוֹן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בְּפֶסַח מִצְרַיִם שֶׁהָיָה נֶאֱכָל בְּחִפָּזוֹן, וְלֹא פֶּסַח דּוֹרוֹת. מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהַהַתְחָלָה לְנַתֵּק עַצְמוֹ מִכָּל תַּאֲווֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא מְקֻשָּׁר בָּהֶם, צָרִיךְ לִשְׁמֹר הָרֶגַע שֶׁמִּתְעוֹרֵר בּוֹ רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם, וְלַחְפּוֹז עַל אוֹתוֹ רֶגַע לְמַהֵר לָצֵאת מֵהֶם, אוּלַי יוּכַל. וְאַחַר כָּךְ שׁוּב יֵלֵךְ בִּמְתִינוּת וּלְאַט, כְּדִין פֶּסַח דּוֹרוֹת.
records.targetEnglish: A person’s first entry into the service of God must be in haste, just as we find that the Passover offering in Egypt was eaten in haste, whereas the Passover offering of later generations was not. At the beginning, to detach oneself from all the desires of this world to which one is bound, one must guard the moment in which the desire for God awakens within, and rush upon that moment to hasten out of them, if perhaps one can. Afterward, one should again proceed with deliberation and slowly, like the law of the Passover offering of later generations.
records.explanation: Rav Tzadok reads the haste of the first Passover as a model for the initial break with entrenched desires. His explicit qualification matters: after seizing the first awakening, service must proceed patiently. The exceptional first Passover is therefore not a demand to rush all later religious life.

records.sourceHebrew: וְנֶאֱכָל בְּחִפָּזוֹן וְכוּ׳. מְנָא לַן? דְּאָמַר קְרָא: ״וַאֲכַלְתֶּם אוֹתוֹ בְּחִפָּזוֹן״. ״אוֹתוֹ״ נֶאֱכָל בְּחִפָּזוֹן, וְאֵין אַחֵר נֶאֱכָל בְּחִפָּזוֹן.
records.sourceEnglish: “And it was eaten in haste,” and so forth. From where do we derive this? Scripture says: “You shall eat it in haste.” That offering is eaten in haste, but no other Passover offering is eaten in haste.
records.targetHebrew: א] רֵאשִׁית כְּנִיסַת הָאָדָם לַעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת בְּחִפָּזוֹן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בְּפֶסַח מִצְרַיִם שֶׁהָיָה נֶאֱכָל בְּחִפָּזוֹן, וְלֹא פֶּסַח דּוֹרוֹת. מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהַהַתְחָלָה לְנַתֵּק עַצְמוֹ מִכָּל תַּאֲווֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא מְקֻשָּׁר בָּהֶם, צָרִיךְ לִשְׁמֹר הָרֶגַע שֶׁמִּתְעוֹרֵר בּוֹ רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם, וְלַחְפּוֹז עַל אוֹתוֹ רֶגַע לְמַהֵר לָצֵאת מֵהֶם, אוּלַי יוּכַל. וְאַחַר כָּךְ שׁוּב יֵלֵךְ בִּמְתִינוּת וּלְאַט, כְּדִין פֶּסַח דּוֹרוֹת.
records.targetEnglish: A person’s first entry into the service of God must be in haste, just as we find that the Passover offering in Egypt was eaten in haste, whereas the Passover offering of later generations was not. At the beginning, to detach oneself from all the desires of this world to which one is bound, one must guard the moment in which the desire for God awakens within, and rush upon that moment to hasten out of them, if perhaps one can. Afterward, one should again proceed with deliberation and slowly, like the law of the Passover offering of later generations.
records.explanation: This is the precise talmudic derivation behind Rav Tzadok’s distinction: “that offering,” the Passover in Egypt, required haste; later Passover offerings did not. He applies that distinction to an urgent first escape from desires followed by deliberate, gradual service.

records.sourceHebrew: וְכָ֘כָה֮ תֹּאכְל֣וּ אֹתוֹ֒ מׇתְנֵיכֶ֣ם חֲגֻרִ֔ים נַֽעֲלֵיכֶם֙ בְּרַגְלֵיכֶ֔ם וּמַקֶּלְכֶ֖ם בְּיֶדְכֶ֑ם וַאֲכַלְתֶּ֤ם אֹתוֹ֙ בְּחִפָּז֔וֹן פֶּ֥סַח ה֖וּא לַיהֹוָֽה׃
records.sourceEnglish: This is how you shall eat it: your waist girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand. You shall eat it in haste; it is a Passover offering to the LORD.
records.targetHebrew: והנה מצוה הראשונה הי' אכילת פסחים שהוא לאכול בשר קודש וכל א' מישראל יכנס בו קדושה מזה. ובא בו המצוה וככה תאכלו אותו ? נעלכם ברגלכם ומקלכם בידכם. ולמה הוצרכו לזה והלא האכילה הי' בלילה ויצ"מ ביום. אך זהו ההכנה שמזומנים ללכת אחרי ד' לכתך אחרי במדבר. וזהו מ"ש ברגל ימין, שעסק חודש זה להיות מוכן ללכת אחרי ד' והלכת בדרכיו וזהו קבלת עומ"ש שהיא ה' אחרונה מלכות
records.targetEnglish: The first commandment was the eating of the paschal offerings: to eat sacred meat, so that holiness would enter every Israelite through it. The commandment given concerning it was: “This is how you shall eat it—your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand.” Why did they need this, when the eating took place at night and the departure from Egypt by day? Rather, this was the preparation of being ready to follow the LORD: “your following Me into the wilderness.” This is the meaning of “the right foot”: the work of this month is to be ready to follow the LORD, “to walk in His ways.” This is accepting the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, represented by the final letter heh, kingship.
records.explanation: Rav Tzadok asks why the Israelites had to eat dressed for travel when they would not depart until daytime. His answer identifies the inner act beneath the haste: readiness to follow God before the journey has begun. This illuminates the first awakening described in Tzidkat HaTzadik as a concrete act of willingness and preparation.

records.sourceHebrew: וְכָ֘כָה֮ תֹּאכְל֣וּ אֹתוֹ֒ מׇתְנֵיכֶ֣ם חֲגֻרִ֔ים נַֽעֲלֵיכֶם֙ בְּרַגְלֵיכֶ֔ם וּמַקֶּלְכֶ֖ם בְּיֶדְכֶ֑ם וַאֲכַלְתֶּ֤ם אֹתוֹ֙ בְּחִפָּז֔וֹן פֶּ֥סַח ה֖וּא לַיהֹוָֽה׃
records.sourceEnglish: This is how you shall eat it: your waist girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand. You shall eat it in haste; it is a Passover offering to the LORD.
records.targetRef: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 25:1
records.targetHebrew: וזאת הכל מורה שבמקום כזה שישראל מכירין מפורש את רצונו ית' אז אינם משגיחין שוב על שום סדר ויש להם קפיצין לדלג בלי שום הדרגה רק בגודל זריזות לעשות רצונו ית' וזה הוא פסח שהי' אבותינו אוכלים וכו' על שום מה על שום שפסח הקב"ה וכו' היינו מפני מה נצטוו על עבודה חזקה כזאת על שום שפסח הקב"ה על בתי אבותינו במצרים וכו' היינו משום שפסח הקב"ה ג"כ והאיר לנו הישועה באורח דילוג בחפזון בלא זמנא ע"כ נצטווינו ונקבע בלבינו ג"כ לעשות עבודה כזו בזמן קצר ובגודל זריזות:
records.targetEnglish: All this indicates that, in a situation where Israel clearly recognizes His blessed will, they no longer attend to any established order, but have the capacity to leap without proceeding through gradual stages, acting with great alacrity to do His blessed will. This is the meaning of: “The Passover offering that our ancestors would eat—for what reason? Because the Holy One, blessed be He, passed over.” That is, why were they commanded to undertake such intense service? “Because the Holy One, blessed be He, passed over the houses of our ancestors in Egypt”: because the Holy One, blessed be He, also leapt over, and shone salvation upon us by a leap, in haste, before the appointed time. Therefore we too were commanded, and it was fixed in our hearts, to perform such service in a short time and with great alacrity.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the reciprocal movement of Passover: God brings rescue by a leap before the normal stages are complete, and Israel answers with swift service when His will becomes clear. This directly enriches Rav Tzadok’s account of seizing the first awakening. It describes this particular moment of clear divine will; it does not abolish the later work of gradual development.

records.sourceHebrew: חֲמִשָּׁה אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים, אֵלּוּ הֵן: אֵשׁ, דְּבַשׁ, וְשַׁבָּת, וְשֵׁינָה, וַחֲלוֹם. אֵשׁ — אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים לְגֵיהִנָּם. דְּבַשׁ — אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים לַמָּן. שַׁבָּת — אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא. שֵׁינָה — אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים לַמִּיתָה. חֲלוֹם — אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים לַנְּבוּאָה.
records.sourceEnglish: Five things are one-sixtieth of something else: fire, honey, Shabbat, sleep, and a dream. Fire is one-sixtieth of Gehinnom. Honey is one-sixtieth of manna. Shabbat is one-sixtieth of the World to Come. Sleep is one-sixtieth of death. A dream is one-sixtieth of prophecy.
records.targetHebrew: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם נז:): חֲלוֹם אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים בִּנְבוּאָה, וְכֵן שַׁבָּת אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁקְּצָת טַעַם נִרְגָּשׁ גַּם כֵּן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, כְּעִנְיַן אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים שֶׁהוּא הַתְחָלַת הַרְגָּשַׁת הַטַּעַם הַיּוֹתֵר מוּעָט, כִּי אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים וְאֶחָד אֵין טַעַם, וְהַתְחָלָתוֹ אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים. כִּי הַמַּעֲשִׂים הֵם רוֹשְׁמִים מוּעָטִים לַאֲמִיתַּת הַנְּקוּדָּה שֶׁבַּלֵּב הַנֶּעְלָם.
records.targetEnglish: Nevertheless, our Sages of blessed memory said: a dream is one-sixtieth of prophecy, and similarly Shabbat is one-sixtieth of the World to Come. A little of its taste is also felt in this world, like one-sixtieth, which is the beginning of the slightest perception of taste: at one part in sixty-one there is no taste, while its beginning is one part in sixty. For deeds are faint impressions of the truth of the hidden point within the heart.
records.explanation: Rav Tzadok explains the specific fraction “one-sixtieth” through the threshold at which a trace of taste can be perceived. Shabbat gives a real but minimal taste of a reality that ordinary experience does not fully reveal. This supplies an interpretation of the talmudic image rather than merely repeating that Shabbat resembles the World to Come.

records.sourceEnglish: Five things are one-sixtieth of something else: fire, honey, Shabbat, sleep, and a dream. Fire is one-sixtieth of Gehinnom. Honey is one-sixtieth of manna. Shabbat is one-sixtieth of the World to Come. Sleep is one-sixtieth of death. A dream is one-sixtieth of prophecy.
records.targetHebrew: וְדָבָר זֶה הוּא הַקִּבּוּל שָׂכָר שֶׁבְּיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת, שֶׁהוּא מֵעֵין הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, עַל מַעֲשָׂיו בַּפּוֹעַל בְּשֵׁשֶׁת יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה. וְכָל הֲנָאַת עוֹלָם הַבָּא הוּא שֶׁנֶּהֱנִין מִזִּיו הַשְּׁכִינָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בְּרָכוֹת יז סוֹף עַמּוּד א), וְכָךְ לַזּוֹכִים לִטְעוֹם בְּשַׁבָּת אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא (בְּרָכוֹת נז:),
records.targetEnglish: This is the receiving of reward on Shabbat, which is a foretaste of the World to Come, for the deeds actually performed during the six working days. All the enjoyment of the World to Come consists in enjoying the radiance of the Divine Presence, as stated in Berakhot 17a. The same applies to those who merit to taste on Shabbat one-sixtieth of the World to Come, as stated in Berakhot 57b.
records.explanation: Rav Tzadok identifies the content of this Shabbat “taste”: enjoyment of the Divine Presence, not simply relief from physical labor. His concluding condition makes the connection practical and precise: the rest a person can receive corresponds to the spiritual work of the preceding weekdays.

records.sourceHebrew: וַיְבָ֤רֶךְ אֱלֹהִים֙ אֶת־י֣וֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִ֔י וַיְקַדֵּ֖שׁ אֹת֑וֹ כִּ֣י ב֤וֹ שָׁבַת֙ מִכׇּל־מְלַאכְתּ֔וֹ אֲשֶׁר־בָּרָ֥א אֱלֹהִ֖ים לַעֲשֽׂוֹת׃
records.sourceEnglish: God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it He ceased from all His work that God had created to do.
records.targetHebrew: וְגַם בִּרְכַּת הַשַּׁבָּת אִיתָא (בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פֶּרֶק יא, ב): בֵּרְכוֹ בַּמָּן, שֶׁהָיָה בַּשִּׁשִּׁי לֶחֶם מִשְׁנֶה, וְזוֹ הַבְּרָכָה בְּיוֹם ו'. אֲבָל אֵין הַבְּרָכָה בּוֹ מִצַּד עַצְמוֹ, רַק מִצַּד מַה שֶּׁנַּעֲשָׂה בּוֹ הֲכָנָה לְיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת; וּבִרְכַּת הַשַּׁבָּת הִיא מִתְפַּשֶּׁטֶת וּמִתְגַּלֵּית וְיוֹצְאָה לַפּוֹעַל בּוֹ. וְשַׁבָּת נִקְרָא "מְקוֹר הַבְּרָכוֹת" כִּי כָּל בְּרָכָה בְּעַצְמוּתָהּ הוּא בְּלֹא שׁוּם מַעֲשֶׂה כְּלָל: וּכְמוֹ הַבְּרָכָה דְּמָן שֶׁנִּמְצָא בְּיוֹם ו' לֶחֶם מִשְׁנֶה – הֵם לֹא לָקְטוּ יוֹתֵר מִמַּה שֶּׁלָּקְטוּ בְּכָל יוֹם, וְאַף נְפִילַת הַמָּן מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם לֹא הָיָה יוֹתֵר מִבְּכָל יוֹם, רַק שֶׁבִּמְדִידַת הַלְּקִיטָה מָצְאוּ יוֹתֵר; וְנִמְצָא בְּעַצְמוּת הַבְּרָכָה לֹא הָיָה שׁוּם פְּעֻלָּה וּמַעֲשֶׂה, אֶלָּא שֶׁלְּעִנְיַן חָלוּת וְהַשְׁרָאַת הַבְּרָכָה אִי אֶפְשָׁר בְּרֵיקַנְיָא, רַק צָרִיךְ אֵיזֶה דָּבָר בַּפּוֹעַל וּפְעֻלָּה כָּל שֶׁהוּא דְּאָדָם שֶׁעַל זֶה תָּחוּל הַבְּרָכָה, שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹצֶה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הַכֹּל עַל יְדֵי הָאָדָם הֶעָשׂוּי בַּדּוּגְמָא הָעֶלְיוֹנָה.
records.targetEnglish: Regarding the blessing of Shabbat, too, Genesis Rabbah 11:2 says that He blessed it through the manna: on the sixth day there was a double portion of bread, so this blessing occurred on Friday. But the blessing was not in Friday for its own sake; it came because preparation for Shabbat took place on that day. The blessing of Shabbat spreads into Friday, becomes revealed, and comes into actuality there. Shabbat is called “the source of blessings,” because blessing in its essence involves no action at all. In the blessing of the manna, when a double portion was found on Friday, they did not gather more than they gathered each day, nor did more manna fall from heaven than on any other day. Rather, when they measured what they had gathered, they found more. Thus no action or deed occurred in the blessing itself. However, for the blessing to take effect and rest upon something, it cannot do so in emptiness: there must be something actual, some action, however small, by a person, upon which the blessing can rest. For the blessed God desires everything to come through the human being, who was made in the likeness of the supernal pattern.
records.explanation: Rav Tzadok resolves how a day of ceasing from work can be the source of blessing. The blessing is a divine gift, while weekday preparation supplies the vessel in which it appears. The double portion of manna therefore manifests Shabbat’s blessing before Shabbat begins.

records.sourceHebrew: כִּדְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר. דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: אוֹר שֶׁבָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּיוֹם רִאשׁוֹן, אָדָם צוֹפֶה בּוֹ מִסּוֹף הָעוֹלָם וְעַד סוֹפוֹ. כֵּיוָן שֶׁנִּסְתַּכֵּל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל וּבְדוֹר הַפְּלַגָּה וְרָאָה שֶׁמַּעֲשֵׂיהֶם מְקוּלְקָלִים — עָמַד וּגְנָזוֹ מֵהֶן, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וְיִמָּנַע מֵרְשָׁעִים אוֹרָם״. וּלְמִי גְּנָזוֹ — לַצַּדִּיקִים לֶעָתִיד לָבֹא, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וַיַּרְא אֱלֹהִים אֶת הָאוֹר כִּי טוֹב״, וְאֵין ״טוֹב״ אֶלָּא צַדִּיק, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״אִמְרוּ צַדִּיק כִּי טוֹב״.
records.sourceEnglish: This follows Rabbi Elazar, who said: With the light that the Holy One, blessed be He, created on the first day, Adam could see from one end of the world to the other. When the Holy One, blessed be He, looked upon the generation of the Flood and the generation of the Dispersion and saw that their deeds were corrupt, He arose and hid it from them, as it is said: “Their light is withheld from the wicked.” For whom did He hide it? For the righteous in the future, as it is said: “God saw the light, that it was good”; and “good” means a righteous person, as it is said: “Say of the righteous that it is good.”
records.targetHebrew: כְּשֶׁמַּתְחִיל הָאָדָם לִכְנוֹס לְתוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב, אָז הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר לוֹ מְאֹד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "פֵּתַח דְּבָרֶיךָ יָאִיר מֵבִין פְּתָיִים]" (תְּהִלִּים קיט, קל). וְכָל הַמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת וּרְצוֹנוֹת לְתוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה נִקְרָא "דְּבָרֶיךָ", שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְדַבֵּר עִם הָאָדָם, וְאֵלּוּ הַמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת נַעֲשִׂים מִזֶּה. וּבַפְּתִיחָה יָאִיר מְאֹד, שֶׁזֶּה "מֵבִין פְּתָיִים", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בִּשְׁמוֹת רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה ג) דְּקוֹרִין לְיָנוֹקָא פַּתְיָא; וּבְהַתְחָלַת הָעֲבוֹדָה נִקְרָא כָּל אֶחָד "נַעַר", וּלְהַהַתְחָלַת הֲבָנָה צָרִיךְ אוֹר גָּדוֹל, וְאַחַר כָּךְ מִסְתַּלֵּק, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק זֶה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ג): זֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: בְּרֵאשִׁית וְכוּלֵי וַיְהִי אוֹר, וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: אוֹר שֶׁבָּרָא וְכוּלֵי גְּנָזוֹ; וְהִנֵּה לָמָּה בְּרָאוֹ? עַל כָּרְחֲךָ הַצֹּרֶךְ כָּךְ: שֶׁיִּבָּרֵא וְיִגָּנֵז. וְכֵן בְּעֵת מַתַּן תּוֹרָה נֶאֱמַר: "אֲנִי אָמַרְתִּי אֱלֹהִים אַתֶּם וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים פב, ו), שֶׁהָיָה אָז "פֵּתַח דְּבָרֶיךָ", וְאַחַר כָּךְ נִסְתַּלֵּק עַד לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר. וְהָעֵצָה לָזֶה – תְּפִלָּה
records.targetEnglish: When a person begins to enter Torah and the service of the heart, the blessed God shines upon that person very greatly, as it is written: “The opening of Your words gives light; it gives understanding to the simple.” All thoughts and desires for Torah and service are called “Your words”: the blessed God speaks with the person, and these thoughts arise from this. At the opening He shines very greatly. This is “giving understanding to the simple,” as Shemot Rabbah, chapter 3, says that a child is called petaya. At the beginning of service everyone is called a youth, and the beginning of understanding requires a great light; afterward it departs. This is as our Sages said about this verse: “In the beginning,” and “Let there be light”; and they said that He hid away the light He created. Why, then, did He create it? Necessarily this was what was required: that it be created and then hidden away. Similarly, at the giving of the Torah it was said: “I said, you are divine beings.” That was then “the opening of Your words”; afterward it departed, until the future, when it will return. The counsel for this is prayer.
records.explanation: Rav Tzadok asks why the primordial light was created if it was then hidden, and reads that order as the pattern of spiritual beginnings: a great illumination opens understanding, then withdraws. This helps explain both the urgency of a first awakening and the patient work afterward. His stated response to the withdrawal is prayer, so the quotation preserves that conclusion.
